Toronto, Canada, ]une 1965

THE 


FUTURE 

LOOK 

Increased Participation 

Participation in the camping move¬ 
ment is increasing annually in Canada. 
More people are taking an active part 
in camp leadership and camp commit¬ 
tee work, and more of our Canadian 
youth are taking advantage of the fine 
programme offered by a wide variety 
of agencies, groups and individuals. 
There are over 1,600 camps in Canada 
today servicing at least 500,000 
campers. 

Public interest is growing, and with 
it, an awareness by many of us, both 
east and west, that camping is taking 
its rightful place as a major contribu¬ 
tor to the mature growth of children 
and young adults in Canada. Federal 
and provincial assistance to camping 
associations is playing an important 
role in the development of qualified 
leaders. Provincial associations are 
working in close co-operation with 
provincial departments in order to 
initiate or maintain standards in the 
areas of accreditation and licensing. 

Present Trends 

In a recent article in the Camping 
Magazine of the American Camping 
Association *(#1), William E. Brat- 
tain comments on the results of a 



by W. D. Smith, Ed.D. 
Immediate Past President, 
Canadian Camping Association 


survey taken to evaluate the general 
course of today’s camping. Over 
ninety per cent of the respondents 
agreed on the following seven points: 

Programmes are becoming more 
flexible, with less adherence to 
formal class type schedules and 
more opportunity for change . . . 
trip and travel camping is on the 
upgrade . . . better trained and 
more mature counsellors, particu¬ 
larly leaders with group leader¬ 
ship skills, are sought by camp 
administrators . . . the need for 
establishing basic personnel and 
professional requirements for camp 
directors seems more and more 
apparent . . . camps are concerned 
with both facility and programme 
development . . . administrators 
are increasingly aware of meeting 
certain standards . . . various gov¬ 
ernmental agencies have increased 
controls in camping, especially in 
regard to legal controls and health 
and safety requirements. 

In all likelihood, the majority of 
these apply to Canadian camping but 
I wonder if we are keeping pace with 
personnel and professional require¬ 
ments for camp directors, meeting 
certain standards, or the increased 


124 


Canadian Camping 



controls for health, safety require¬ 
ments and legal liability. 

Kirk Wipper, of the University of 
Toronto in addressing the Nova Scotia 
Camping Association (#2) during 
their 1964 Camp Directors’ Seminar 
suggested several facility trends. They 
should be favourably considered for 
camp maintenance and development. 
One involves the use of plastic material 
such as plastic pipe for water lines 
and fibre glass for screening as well 
as boat structure and repairs. Another 
indicated a new and modern, contem¬ 
porary architecture of camp buildings 
designed by specialists in the field. 

Problem Areas 

In addition he outlined several prob¬ 
lems that camp owners and associations 
should attempt to solve in program¬ 
ming. Why do the majority of children 
start camping at the age of nine and 
stop at the age of thirteen? Why is 
there such a large segment of boys and 
girls in this country who have no 
camping experiences open to them? 
We should find answers to these ques¬ 
tions in the immediate future or we 
are not facing up to our responsi¬ 
bilities. 


The Future 

The future look in camping will see 
an increase in fees and counsellor’s 
wages. Camp personnel will have bet¬ 
ter qualifications but it will require 
more extensive training—in-service by 
the camp, graded standards by pro¬ 
vincial associations and national leader¬ 
ship schools for selected individuals. 

There will be a better evaluation of 
what actually takes place at camp. 
Changes in campers will be measured 
objectively and research will give 
some indication of what programmes 
are necessary to foster improvement. 


Attitude changes, an awareness of 
inter-cultural understanding and 
better human relations fostered 
through camping experiences will be 
emphasized. 

Individual camps will look back long 
enough to record a history of their 
development and a more precise out¬ 
line of their own particular philosophy. 
Camp folders and brochures of the 
future will be more individualistic and 
stress their own camp philosophy and 
history. The era of publications adver¬ 
tising camp openings in dreary, uni¬ 
formity, where all literature sounds 
the same no matter what camp it 
represents, should be replaced. 

There will be greater use of public 
lands for resident camps and a better 
conception of the conservation of our 
resources for tomorrow. Small areas 
will be leased with permission to use 
and develop adjoining parkland and 
conservation regions. New programmes 
of outpost camping will augment those 
currently offered and define more 
exactly the differences between de¬ 
centralized and outpost camping. 

Camp programmes for teen-agers 
will be studied and evaluated in order 
to increase participation by the cur¬ 
rently diminishing group of the “in- 
betweeners” — neither children nor 
adults. It will require concerted effort 
and co-operation by sociologists, psy¬ 
chologists, social workers and camp 
personnel to make any inroads on the 
problem. 

Church camps will increase their 
residence time to a minimum of two 
weeks with voluntary staff gradually 
being replaced by paid leaders in the 
roles of administration and super¬ 
vision. The important job of the 
volunteer will require more training, 
greater recruiting and a better under- 


Toronto, Canada, June 1965 


125 



standing of the interests, needs and 
group interaction of campers. 

Provincial Associations 

Let me re-affirm some implications 
for the future originally outlined at: 
the 1963 Institute of the Manitoba 
Camping Association (#3) in an 
address on Leadership in Camping: 

Provincially, more of our asso¬ 
ciations should be doing some¬ 
thing about: a provincial charter, 
legislation for tax relief, con¬ 
servation, provincial parks, school 
camping and year-round use of 
facilities ... is there a need for 
the study and development of day 
camp and family camp standards? 
Should we compile statistics on the 
number of camps and campers that 
the association represents? Should 
information booklets on camping 
areas and resources be published 
provincially? Nationally? 

I would anticipate that these and 
many others will be realized in the 
next decade if we are to keep pact! 
with recent developments. 

Nationally, the Canadian Camping 
Association can expect to face prob¬ 
lems of expansion and a general self- 
evaluation of the part it can and 
should play in the development of 
camping in Canada. Federal grants 
for projects will tend to unite provin¬ 
cial associations in a common purpose 
and goal. The C.C.A. constitution will 
be revised with greater emphasis on 
bi-cultural and bi-lingual understand¬ 
ing. Some conflicts will arise because 
of the increased fee structure forcing 
us to hasten the self-evaluation pro¬ 
cedure. 

There is a trend towards biennial 
meetings of the association with reg¬ 
ional or provincial meetings replacing 
the annual sessions. The cross country 


journey as a centennial project will 
re-awaken the pioneering spirit of 
travel by the early fur traders and 
unite provincial associations in a com¬ 
mon cause. Inter - cultural under¬ 
standing through camper and coun¬ 
sellor exchange programmes will be 
evaluated to clearly indicate that atti¬ 
tudes and appreciations for the differ¬ 
ent cultures in Canada can be changed 
in the camp setting. Foreign students 
under the External Aid Program of 
the Government of Canada will make 
a contribution to the camp experiences 
of our youth under a voluntary assist¬ 
ance program co-ordinated by the 
C.C.A. 

Publications on camping will in¬ 
crease in scope and an annual directory 
of Canadian camps, camping areas 
and facilities will supplement the 
literature in the field. 


The Challenge 

It is a time of change — a change 
so rapid that it is difficult to keep pace. 
If we can eliminate the petty problems 
of the past, if we can continue to 
emphasize the service to others, if we 
can develop an all-Canadian unity of 
purpose and endeavour, and if we 
believe it is so important that we can¬ 
not fail — then and only then, will 
camping assume its rightful place as 
a major contributing factor to the 
fullest development of Canadian youth. 

REFERENCES 

1. Brattain, William E. “Take a Look at 
Camping—Its Current, Future Trends”, 
Camping Magazine, American Camp¬ 
ing Association. Vol. 36, No. 9, Novem- 
ber-December, 1964. 

2. Wippcr, Kirk A. W. “Leadership—the 
Key to Camping”, Camp Directors’ 
Seminar and Camp Leadership Course. 
Nova Scotia Camping Association, 1964. 

3. Smith, W. Donald. “Leadership In 
Camping”, 1963 Institute of the Mani¬ 
toba Camping Association. M.C.A., 
Winnipeg. 1963.

Canadian Camping 



Give Your Heart to the Children . . . 

Whether in Day or Resident Camp 

by Shirley Hall 


Give your heart to the children and 
give your brain to organization. 

The heritage of our country is 
steeped in a glorious history of out¬ 
doors and outdoor living. The Indians, 
voyageurs, fur traders, pioneers, mis¬ 
sionaries and settlers all depended upon 
their knowledge and skill in the use 
and conservation of nature and learned 
that conservation was the very essence 
of their existence. This heritage must 
be passed on to the children of today 
who are ready and eager to experience 
outdoor life because of their imagina¬ 
tion and adventurous spirit. Many 
children of today have little knowledge 
of the wonders of nature and the joy 
of outdoor living. The environment of 
crowded apartments, subdivisions, small 
gardens, few trees and small families 
is not conducive to a happy, group out¬ 
door living experience. Some fortu¬ 
nate children are able to go far away 
from the crowded city to a resident 
camp for two, or more, weeks each 
summer, but many must stay at home 
and try to fill the summer days with 
worthwhile activity. It is to these 
“pavement-bound” children that Day 
Camping can be of value. 

There are many excellent pro¬ 
grammes of activity and interest offered 
to “pavement-bound” children during 
the summer months—supervised play¬ 
grounds, sports clinics, craft clubs, 
swimming lessons, tours of local points 
of interest — but Day Camping is 
unique in that its relationship to, and 
use of, the out-of-doors is the focal 
point. And so, we move out of the 


church basements, school playgrounds 
and areas hemmed in by city sights, 
smells and noises to campsites where 
the campers are surrounded by hills, 
ravines, trees, fields, flowers, birds, 
insects, space, and a pond or stream. 
What we do when we move into this 
wonderfully free atmosphere of out¬ 
door living is what makes the difference 
between a real day camp experience 
and any other programme which could 
be equally well offered in a building 
or playground. We leave behind the 
baseballs and bats, the tennis racquets, 
the paper crafts, the record player, the 
mosaic tile and the plasticene and we 
learn to camp and enjoy and respect 
nature. 

Hiking, woodlore, nature lore, cook¬ 
ery, campcraft, archery, woodcraft pio¬ 
neer and Indian lore can be offered in 
most Day Camps. Swimming can also 
be offered in many Day Camps. These 
arc basic skills which are a real part 
of outdoor living and many pro¬ 
grammes full of fun and adventure 
develop from them—skits, crafts, crea¬ 
tive drama, wide games, overnight 
sleep-outs, tracking and Pow-wows, to 
name a very few. 

Campers should be introduced to 
these camp skills so that they have 
meaning in living a comfortable life 
out-of-doors and so that the campers 
understand the “why” of learning and 
doing the various projects. A leader 
with his new group of eight or ten 
campers will encourage his group to 
find a suitable, comfortable campsite 
within the day camp area. This is the 


Toronto, Canada, June 1965 


127 




time to explore the camp area with 
the campers; have them suggest various 
campsites: point out why this gully 
could be unsuitable in damp weather 
or why under that big half-dead elm 
may not be a safe place on windy 
days. Once the campers have chosen 
their special campsite try to have them 
suggest who will be needed in or near 
the campsite so that we may be com¬ 
fortable and will make our outdoor 
living easier. Oh, we would like to 
have a fire! What for — for cooking, 
for warmth, for the simple pleasure of 
sitting around our own fire singing 
songs or telling stories? For all these 
reasons! Fine, then there are many 
things we must learn about many dif¬ 
ferent types of fires! But, first of all. 
we must be aware of fire safety. Why 
can’t we just build a fire any place in 
our campsite? Yes, fires can be danger¬ 
ous unless properly prepared! This is 
the time to teach the campers about 
turfing, or choosing a sandy area, and 
choosing a place free of hazards such 
as low-hanging branches, and the 
necessity of having easy access to 
water or sand for extinguishing the 
fire. 

Our first project is to be a cooking 
fire. Maybe we can find flat rocks to 
build up a shelf on either side of the 
fire for balancing our cooking pots and 
pans. Possibly we should dig a small 
trench and construct a trench fire. The 
counsellor can point out the merits of 
various types of cooking fires; show the 
children how to prepare for them and 
let them do the building. Now, we 
need wood and kindling for our fire. 
What kind of wood; where can we 
find it, what kinds of materials are best 
for kindling? This is a perfect time to 
make the children aware of the im¬ 
portance of conservation. We never 
destroy or burn living, green trees. 
(Green wood doesn’t burn well, any¬ 
way!) Now, we have our wood col¬ 
lected. Where should we store it? 
What might happen if we placed the 


woodpile where the wind could blow 
the flames onto it? And so our wood 
must be piled safely “up-wind” from 
our fire-site. Now the children can 
be shown the tec-pee fire, the log 
cabin fire. Let them pair off and try 
constructing these fires themselves. A 
water-boiling contest would be fun at 
this point. (Add a few soap chips to 
the can of water and the campers can 
really get the thrill of seeing some¬ 
thing happening when their pot boils.) 
This will point out that their can or 
pot got awfully black and sooty by 
being over the flame, and it is very 
difficult to clean. We don’t want our 
cooking pots and pans to get like that! 
What can be done about it? Let the 
campers soap the outside of a pot and 
see if it is difficult to clean after being 
over a fire. It cleans easily, doesn’t it? 

The campers may have found out 
that their pots should be further away 
from the flames than the trench or 
stone shelves allowed. Fine, we can 
build a tripod or construct a pole 
arrangement between forked sticks. 
The leader of young campers will use 
the hatchet and knife himself, but a 
leader with older children can teach 
them the safe and proper use of these 
potentially dangerous “weapons”. At 
any age the campers must be taught a 
respect for sharp implements and that 
they must never be used without per¬ 
mission and strict supervision. 

What else do we need on our camp¬ 
site? A shelter—for ourselves, for the 
woodpile, for our utensils? Good idea! 
H^w can we build these? The coun¬ 
sellor can show pictures and diagrams 
of various types of shelters; tarpaulin, 
lean-to, etc. This is a perfect time 
to teach lashing, as the campers can 
see its purpose directly in relation to 
what they are building for a useful 
purpose. 

The campers might suggest many 
other things they would like to have at 
their campsite; pot hooks, dish rack, 
“dish pan”, table, seats, cup tree, 


128 


Canadian Camping 



clothes tree. Allow the campers to be 
creative and experimental, but do not 
impose adult standards. 

The group will be eager to cook a 
real meal over their own cooking fire. 
At least one day, and preferably two 
days, before a cook-out discuss with 
the campers what they would like to 
cook for lunch. They may want to 
start simply with weiners on sticks and 
hot chocolate, but later they can be 
led to trying more ambitious menus of 
stew, pancakes or fritters, tin-foil cook¬ 
ery, casseroles, puddings, tea biscuits, 
etc. Send a note home with each 
camper requesting the food item which 
he is to provide on cook-out day. Let 
each camper share in creating the 
meal. Some will build and tend the 
fire, others will help with food prepara¬ 
tion and cooking, and they will all 
have a hand in cleaning up the camp¬ 
site after the meal. Remember, at 
Day Camp you are not trying to win 
an award for outdoor cooking; you are 
trying to feed your campers a whole¬ 
some lunch and teach some of the basic 
cooking skills. 

On your excursions around the camp 
area to collect wood or procure equip¬ 
ment from the camp director the 
campers will be side-tracked many 
times a day by a bird, frog, snake, 
fungus, weed, wild flower, stump, the 
sound of a woodpecker, a cloud forma¬ 
tion, or any one of a million things. 
Let them stop and look at this new 
creature or thing. Take time to ex¬ 
plore this new wonder and discuss it 
with them. If you don’t have the 
answers to their multi-million ques¬ 
tions, have the courage to say, “I don’t 
know, but let’s find out together”. The 
camp director should have a small, but 
good, library available for the coun¬ 
sellors’ use. Exploring the world of 
nature can lead to many other fascinat¬ 
ing projects. Maybe the campers 
would like to build an ant village 
(between two panes of glass) and ob¬ 
serve the “busy-ness” of the ant colony. 


Your group may wish to keep a nature 
diary or a weather chart. Possibly 
they would like to mark a nature trail, 
make a list of all the various kinds of 
trees, wild flowers, or weeds on the 
campsite. The possibilities are only 
limited by the imagination. In dis¬ 
covering acorns or pine cones the girls 
may decide they would like to make 
lapel pins, or necklaces for their Indian 
costumes. Teazles, cattails and milk¬ 
weed pods are marvellous for con¬ 
structing dry bouquets. The boys may 
want to make an Indian tomahawk or 
construct an animal out of queer 
shapes of dried wood or driftwood. 
Again, the possibilities of nature crafts 
are endless. Hikes can be organized 
with a specific purpose in mind: to 
collect pine cones for crafts, to count 
all the oak trees, to follow a stream 
to its source, to find a muskrat hole. 

Naturally, every Day Gamp counsel¬ 
lor will have a well-balanced weekly 
programme planned for his campers 
in order that many new things can be 
experienced and learned, and so that 
every child will have the opportunity 
to accomplish a special skill. The im¬ 
portant thing is to be flexible; change 
the programme on the spur of the 
moment if the weather or campers’ in¬ 
terest dictates a change. Remember, 
day campers return home every eve¬ 
ning full of the adventures of the day. 
Send them home happy! 

The highlight of any Day Camp 
programme is the overnight sleep-out. 
Most of us in Day Camp operation 
have found that children under nine 
years of age are not ready for this 
experience; either emotionally or in the 
realm of skills. This is a special ad¬ 
venture for the older children and a 
“testing” of many camp skills. Now 
the campers must learn to pitch a 
tent. Where is the best place: why? 
Should we trench the tent; why? Show 
the campers these things and let them 
do it with your help. How do we 
page 150 please 


Toronto , Canada, June 1965

PROGRAMME POT-POURRI 

A Little Bit of Everything 


A. CAMPFIRE PROGRAMMES 

What is a Campfire? 

—a get-together for a happy time 
—either a ceremonial or ordinary 
campfire 

—all-camp group or individual cabins 
—fire should be blazing (not smoking) 
—have plenty of firewood handy — 
maybe you could appoint special 
fire-tenders 

—if there is a ban on fires, you could 
place the cabin lanterns around 
the dry campfire. 

Special openings 

1. Medicine Man or Witch Doctor 
could enter and point in the various 
directions of the compass. 

2. Each cabin comes to the campfire 
with a torch. At a certain time the 
camp chief could call on each group 
to place their torch into the fire. 

3. Campfire could be set ahead of 
time with chemical powders and a 
hidden candle. At a special mo¬ 
ment someone could trip a wire 
that is tied around the candle; it 
would fall onto chemicals which 
which would burst into flame. 

4. A wire can be placed from a tree 
to the campfire, and the fire 
soaked in kerosene. At the right 
time, someone hidden in a tree 
will light a tied bundle of rags and 
send them down the wire to the 
campfire. 


by Gordon MacNab 
Vice-President 

Canadian Camping Association 


Coloured flames 

Ingredients: clorin salts, coarse salts, 
bluestone, paraffin wax. 

For red—strontium nitrate 
yellow—calcium nitrate 
green—borax 

purple—potassium chloride 

Use of Singing in Camp 

—unifying influence 
—helps in developing camp theme 
—holds atmosphere in ceremonials 
—a happy camp is a singing camp 

Choice of Songs 

—it’s a good idea to have your pro¬ 
gramme written in advance and 
try to stick to your programme— 
the exception would be, of course, 
informal get-togethers on out- 
trips, evening snacks, etc. 

—song types: introduction, rousing, 
action, slower and then closing 
—do not use song sheets during camp¬ 
fire—learning from them would 
be an excellent programme for 
rest period when they could be 
memorized. 

Song Leading Techniques 

—know the song thoroughly 
—enjoy leading and look as if you are 
enjoying it all; relax and let your¬ 
self go 

—keep the group singing together

—teach the group to watch the tempo 
the leader is giving 

—vary the rhythm (or even the pitch) 
if the song lags. 

—for a smaller group use the camp¬ 
fire circle 

—for a larger group use the horseshoe 
circle—this helps get control and 
attention of all the group 

—stop programme on time — always 
stop when activity is still in high 
interest. If you are in charge, 
have some signal agreed upon 
between you and song-leader. 

—teach one new song each campfire 

—campers and new staff should be 
trained to lead at least half of each 
programme. Remember a fine 
voice isn’t necessary, enthusiasm 
counts for a lot. 

—when teaching a new song, tell a bit 
about its background to set the 
mood; sing it through once (may¬ 
be some of the staff will know if 
and join you) ; then get the 
group doing it, line by line. Don’t 
sing it too often—come back to it 
again next day. 

Remember — songs can be the back¬ 
bone of your campfire — every¬ 
thing can be built around them. 
It helps if someone can accom¬ 
pany on accordion, guitar or other 
instrument. Some evenings there 
will be other activities, but when¬ 
ever there is a campfire make it 
a good one. It should not last 
over an hour, or if there are 
refreshments, a story or stunts, add 
an extra fifteen minutes. 

Divide your Programme as follows: — 

1. Hello Songs—everybody knows all 
the words. 

2. Action Songs—using various parts 
of the body. 

3. Follow after the leader—a great 
favourite. 

4. Rounds. 


5. Special songs with a different 
twist. 

6. Contests, games, skits, action 
stories, special presentations. 

7. Slowing down songs — to settle 
down tempers before bedtime. 

8. Spirituals. 

9. Story or legend. 

10. Closing — end your programme 
with one or two of your camp’s 
special songs or your traditional 
closing—quiet, lifting to the spirit. 

Meals —“off the cuff” singing at meal¬ 
time is good fun, each table 
starting a song and the others 
joining in. 

SPECIAL SECTION OF CAMPFIRE 

1. Icebreakers 

Royal Order of Siam: O wha 
(kneel) Tah noh (hands up) Siam 
(bow). Gather speed “Oh, what an 
ass I am”. Chinese Prayer: everybody 
kneel, bend forward forehead on floor 
repeating “I know my heart, I know 
mv mind, I know that I am stuck up 
behind”. 

Frog Pond: high voices—tomatoes, 
tomatoes, tomatoes; middle voices — 
potatoes, potatoes, potatoes; bass voices 
—fried bacon, fried bacon. Then all 
go at it at once. 

I am a Monkey: series of state¬ 
ments, leader gives the lock. Group 
repeats statement and adds the word 
key. “I am a gold lock” — group — 
“I am a gold key,” “I am a brass lock” 
—“I am a brass key,” “I am a monk 
lock”—I am a Monkey ”. 

Community Sneeze — divide into 3 
groups “Hashce, Hishee, Hoshie”, then 
go it all together. The same with barn¬ 
yard noises, each group a different 
animal. 

2. Contests 

Hand, leg, and wrist wrestles — 
Japanese tugs — knife reaches — talk 


132 


Canadian Camping 



fests — pillow fights — gun, wolf, man 

(for groups)—don’t laugh contests. 

Games: Chip and chop — luggage 
packing — Mathew, Mark, Luke — 
— continuing stories — bear or lion 
hunt — Jacks alive — Indian dances 
— Camp director’s hat — for 
groups: Brutal Miner, Ghost story, 
and small group: Picture drawing— 
skits — comical track meet — Hobo 
bands—Carnivals. 

Yells :—follow the leader. Here are 
some. You can make up some fine 
ones of your own! 

1. Very Good: “Good—Very good— 
Very, very good—Phenomenal!” 

2. Guillotine “Scratch, screech, etc.” 
pulling up blade — “Swish . . . 
swish” blade going down — “Plop” 
head comes off — “Plop, plop, 
plop . . .” head is rolling down 
the street. 

3. Watermelon Swash (make action 
and noise of eating a huge water¬ 
melon)—Yum, yum .(rub tummy) 
spat, spat (spit out seeds). 

4. Ginger Beer Yell Click (top being 
opened)—Clock (remove cork — 
use tongue)—Fizz (beer fizzing) — 
Cluck (sound pouring into the 
glass) Oggle. ogglc (drinking) — 
Ah! (satisfaction). 

5. Mosquito The Buzz (trace flight of 
mosquito with the finger) —,the 
Sting (click with tongue in mouth) 
— the Result (OW!)—the Swat 
(slap hands on knee)—The Cry 
(got him!) 


B. OUTDOOR SPECIAL EVENTS 

Hikes: Exploration — tree, bird, or 
plant identification. Collections—drift¬ 
wood, shells, fungus, insects, berries, 
etc. Meals—early morning hike with 
breakfast; special picnic lunch out¬ 
ing; beach party with swim, cookout 
supper, games. 


Pioneers and Indians — capturing 

scalps. 

Capture the Flag—divide camp into 2 
groups—can be really exciting. 

Sardines—one person hides, as others 
find him they hide with the first 
sardine. 

Kick the Can—excellent in the woods. 

Scavenger Hunt, or a Treasure Hunt, 
and — always popular — a Counsellor 
Hunt. 

Potato Fry—whose is first fire going, 
best onions and potatoes, best clean¬ 
up, who got water boiling first? 

Circus—each cabin puts on an act 
out-of-doors. Could be a parade too. 

Kite Contest—for windy days. Good 
project beforehand, making kites. 

Rodeos, sailing trips, or any of those 
things your camp specializes in. 

Special Projects—nature trails, gates, 
fence, rockwork, dug-outs, a fort. 
Making small sailboats, or cata¬ 
marans (can race them later). 

Campus Games—volleyball, tetherball, 
soccer, lacrosse, softball, touch foot¬ 
ball, horseshoes, and any organized 
small group games such as kick ball, 
ringtoss, wall ball, Chinese soccer 
(grass), dodge ball, crows and cranes, 
streets and alleys, bucketball, broom 
ball, tag games (poison, caboose, 
pirates, chain). 

Operation Marathon — a giant relay 
taking in all camp activities. 

Monks Meal—silent meal, everything 
done with hand and facial expressions, 
dressing up makes it even funier. 

Mock Trial—all in fun, judge, law¬ 
yers, jury, victim, etc.

Nightgown Parade (girls). 

Camper Day—campers take over the 
roles of counsellors and staff. 

Indian Day—or it might be Neptune 
Day in which you could combine all 
related camp activities towards events, 
costumes, decorations, sports. 

Sweat Lodge—find out how to build. 
Great fun sweating in steam, then 
jump in the lake. 

Waterfront Events—A Safari can be a 
combination of hike and boat trip. 
Hold a Fishing Derby — who gets 
smallest fish, biggest, first caught, most 
fish? Have you an Early Morning Dip 
Club (if water warm enough!). Eve¬ 
ning Swims on hot nights, with special 
supervision, are memorable. 

Aquatic Meet—ducking for pebbles or 
eggs, sinkum-sunkum (rowboats with 
buckets), run in shallow water in life 
jackets, jelly floating, feet first swim, 
log rolling, gunwaling, rowboat race 
with hands paddling, rowboat back¬ 
wards, jousting. Relays—wearing rub¬ 
ber boots, egg and spoon, sweat shirt 
change, pingpong ball blow. 

C. INDOOR SPECIAL 
PROGRAMMES, AND 
FOR RAINY DAYS 

Banquet — dress up, tables like hotel 
dinner, elegant menus, special speakers. 

Rain hikes—warm shorts, t-shirts, etc. 
—hot shower, dry clothes afterwards. 

Tournaments — pingpong, checkers, 
roundtable tennis, dominoes, etc. 

Indoor Track Meet—centipede relay, 
scramble for shoes, wind the string, 
shoe box race, balloon blowing, team 
cheers, team songs. 


Talent Night—skits, musicals, talking, 
laughing, whistling contests. 

Masquerade and Girls Fashion Show, 
Charades. 

Camp Newspaper—special edition. 

Camp Craft — making small sailboats 
for when the sun comes out again; 
out - trip gadgets, cabin plaques, 
whistles, hiking sticks, packboards. 

Bingo—all types of ways to win. 

Square Dancing — for girls or mixed 
groups. 

Unbirthday Party — like Alice in 
Wonderland. 

Carnival — set up booths, include 
penny toss, darts, fortune telling. A 
Murder Room for a post mortem 
being done in complete darkness. 
Group sits around the table, you tell 
a story about a man murdered, various 
parts of body have been found and 
arc passed around the group. (Brains 
—wet sponge, head (cabbage), hand 
(glove filled with wet sand), eye 
(peeled grape) veins (wet macaroni) 
teeth (kernels of corn) and so on. 

Cabin Games — campers will have 
some, and many can be found in 
books. You might hold a big games 
day in the dining room. Find out how 
to play Battleship—it is excellent. 

A Rest and Read Period with a special 
distribution of books, encouragement 
to write letters, or do quiet crafts can 
be refreshing change.

Sermon* 

Untier Etje g>utt 


by Eanswythe Flynn, 

Camp Brigadoon 

A Sunday Service, to have any im¬ 
pact at all, should be simple, short, 
musical and cheerful, sincere and free 
of theatricals, a pause in the week to 
give thanks, sing praises and ask for 
a blessing on the camp days ahead. 
Outdoors or in, it is best that some kind 
of musical instrument be used ... a 
portable organ, a piano; or, it might 
be noted that quite realistic organ 
effects can be developed with one or 
two or more Melodicas. Speak to your 
Director of Music. 

This outline, of course, is the sug¬ 
gestion of one camp, can be used only 
as a starting base. 

As campers take their places, the 
music counsellor might play a melody 
of well-known hymn tunes, an anthem, 
appropriate themes from some of the 
great composers’ works. As the music 
ends, the director (or the person in 
charge of the service), standing, can 
set the mood by reading quotations 
from the Old or New Testament. The 
following suggestions give some idea of 
the scope and variety; the choice is as 
large as the Bible itself. 

'‘Let us come before his presence 
with thanksgiving and shew our¬ 
selves glad in Him with psalms.” 

“Great is the Lord, and greatly 
to be praised in the city of our 
God, in the mountain of His 
Holiness.” 

“God is our refuge and our 
strength, a very present help in 
trouble.” 

“The Lord is in His holy 
temple; let all the earth keep 
silence before Him.” 

Follow the reading with the first 
hymn, announced by the Director (still 
standing). Monotony is relieved, inci-

rips and holes 
in all canvas 
camping 
equipment with

Toronto, Canada, June 1965 


135 



dentally, if campers are asked to stand 
for the singing of the hymns. 

After the hymn, the reading of a 
short Psalm which can be read to¬ 
gether, or the Director can read one 
line, the campers the next, and so on 
to the end. Or, if the speaker is 
basing his talk on the Psalm, it is 
quite effective if he (or she) reads it 
alone ... if he is a good reader! 

A Collect or Prayer is said at this 
point, prefaced by the Director’s 
words, “Let us pray”. 

Then, the second hymn, or perhaps 
an Anthem the choir has practiced 
during the week. 

After this, the collection and ad¬ 
dress ... or the collection can be 
made during the hymn after the 
address. 

We cannot emphasize too strongly 
that the address be kept to a minimum. 
IT MUST BE SHORT; no longer 
than ten minutes; in fact, the entire 
service should last no longer than half 
an hour. 

The last hymn follows the talk, a 
closing prayer and the reading of the 
blessing. 

May we suggest the general blessing, 
one that is a favourite and appropriate 
to every denomination, creed or race: 

“The Lord bless us and keep us: 

the Lord lift up the light of his 

countenance upon us, and give us 

peace, now and for ever more.” 

Amen. 


AT SPLIT ROCK FALLS 

by Raymond Souster 

At Split Rock Falls I first saw my death 
In a sudden slip the space of a breath. 

My windmill body met the crazy shock 
Of uncounted centuries of stubborn rock. 

At Split Rock Falls I saw green so green 
It was as though grass had never been; 

In the dappled depths of that pure pool 
My face looked at me, recognized a fool. 

From Split Rock Falls as I came away 
The hint of a rainbow topped the spray: 
And the trees tossed down: O let nothing 
matter 

If not beautiful, swift as that singing water.

MANITOBA 

We received these words of appreciation 
from Kirk A. W. Wipper, University of 
Toronto, School of Physical Education , and 
director of Camp Kandalore, Ontario, who 
participated in the Conference. Our con¬ 
gratulations, Manitoba! 

It was an inspiring experience to 
visit with Manitoba camping enthusi¬ 
asts on March 19th and 20th, to share 
in the Conference conducted on the 
University of Manitoba campus. 

The Conference was sponsored by 
the Manitoba Camping Association in 
co-operation with the Fitness and 
Amateur Sport Branch. Department of 
Welfare, Province of Manitoba. The 
theme, “Looking at Svhys’ of Camp¬ 
ing” included discussions on philosophy, 
structure and programming in camp. 
The willingness of the confrcrccs to 
share and explore the foundations for 
each camping operation represented, 
regardless of obvious differences, speaks 
well for the Manitoba Camping Asso¬ 
ciation, and for all of Canadian 
camping! 

When one witnesses the enthusiasm 
and dedication of camping leaders, it is 
no small wonder that camping is a 
major force for the training and in¬ 
spiration of children and young people 
in so many parts of Canada. 

In the discussion groups which fol¬ 
lowed the theme addresses, an attempt 
was made to apply philosophical, struc¬ 
tural and programme ideas according 
to the special characteristics of the 
camps involved. This pattern proved 
to be stimulating, and permitted the 
effective participation of a wide variety 
of camps. 

It was indeed a happy venture to 
travel east to the Nova Scotia Camp¬ 
ing Association one year ago and it 
was a further privilege in 1965 to be 
part of the Camping Association of 
Manitoba, my home province. 


QUEBEC 

In one of Canada’s largest daily 
newspapers there appeared during 
March in Nathan Cohen’s column 
these observations (which he has since 
acknowledged must have been based 
on misleading information.) In it he 
stated “A major crisis has developed 
in the Canadian Camping Association 
... As its 1967 centennial project . . . 
the G.C.A. plans to have boys and 
girls travel by canoe along the coast- 
to-coast routes taken by the early 
explorers, and mark these routes. By 
virtue of its history and size, Quebec 
has the longest routes to be travelled 
and marked. But Quebec has a small 
summer camp population. Its sum¬ 
mer camp industry can’t possibly 
handle its share of the project ... If 
Quebec tries to go it alone, the project 
has to fail. If the other provinces 
insist on helping (and he says they 
have offered to but Quebec rejected 
such an idea), Quebec will withdraw 
—either way the Canadian Camping 
Association is wrecked.” 

The following are the main points 
stressed by Mr. Bob La/anik, President 
of Quebec Camping Association, in a 
letter sent to Mr. Cohen. It is good 
that we should all know Quebec’s 
stand on these matters. 

“Mr. Cohen, I am indeed taken 
aback by the information in your 
column. Firstly, there is not at the 
present time, nor has there ever been 
a “major crisis” in our Canadian 
Camping Association, and certainly 
not about our Centennial Project, a 
coast-to-coast canoe trip. 

“As a matter of fact, this was dis¬ 
cussed at the annual meeting of C.C.A. 
held on March 12th, in Vancouver, 
and not only is this the biggest and 
most exciting project ever undertaken 
by C.C.A., but it also is serving to 
draw together more closely the various 
provincial sections. Not only is our

SPECIAL WATERFRONT PROGRAMMES 

by Ron Mayeda Camp Kandalore 

Ron set out the following as an outline with which to develop discussion at 
his session at the Ontario Camping Conference in February. We thought it so 
comprehensive that we feel sure it will help with your waterfront programming 
just as it stands. 

REGATTAS 

(a) Mechanics: 

The motto of all regattas should be “Maximum activity and maximum 
participation.” 

1. Teams 

—chosen before the actual day 
—captains chosen before the actual day 
*—attempt made to balance the teams 
—do we have permanent or non-permanent teams 
—choosing the name for the team 

—how many teams do we have (maximum participation) 

—do we use the same teams for other camp activities 
—are the captains staff members or senior campers 
—will the staff be assigned to the teams 

2. Interest 

—sportsmanship vs. winning 
—team cheers, songs and banners 
—true competitive atmosphere 

—results announced to the whole camp. Recognize team effort not 
individuals 

—events are known in advance 

3. Details 

—officials obtained (CIT’s, instructors, counsellors) 

—list of equipment needed prepared 
—the events have been explained to the campers 
—make sure that even the poor swimmers have an event 
—provide a meeting place for the team to plan and organize 
—method of scoring determined and posted 
—the value of a split regatta for large camps 
—use only competitive events (no novelty races) 

—have numerous relays 

—establish a swimming course and canoeing course (if possible 
have lanes) 

4. Suggested two hour programme 
Swimming (Sr. Dock) 

1. Int. 50 yd. free 

2. Sr. 50 yd. free 

3. Int. 50 yd. back 

4. Sr. 50 yd. back 

5. Open 200 yd. free 

6. Int. free relay 

7. Sr. free relay 


Canoeing (Sr. dock) 

1. Int. canoe doubles 

2. Sr. canoe doubles 

3. Int. canoe fours 

4. Sr. canoe fours 

5. Int. kayak 

6. Sr. kayak 

7. War canoe race 


Toronto, Canada, June 1965 


141 


Naturally we can swim back one week, breast the next and perhaps 
butterfly. The free relays on alternate weeks could become medley 
relays. 

Other alternatives—sailing takes place in the morning. 

Staff* races (no more than two) could be included for interest. 


Canoeing 

1. 3 man crab race (ns) 
3 man crab race 
canoe doubles 
canoe fours 
canoe tug-of-war (ns) 
War canoe race 


Swimming (Jr. dock) 

1. Walk, run, crawl, fly 

2. 50 yd. free 

3. 50 yd. back 

4. 1 length free relay 
(W,R,C,F) 

5. free relay 
5. Suggested officials 

-—canoe and swim starter 
—four finish judges 
-—announcer 
—scorckeeper 

—lifeguards (one per team) 

(b) Safety: 

—each team must supply one lifeguard 
—have one or two of waterfront staff as lifeguards 
—row boat needed to guard canoe races 
—stress no dumping during canoe races (especially staff) 

—do not allow any horseplay during regatta 

—OBEY ALL WATER SAFETY RULES AT ALL TIMES 


—do not use safety equipment for event 
—the waterfront director should be assigned no specific job. 

He is the trouble shooter. 

—restrict decks to officials only 

—make sure that staff are with the campers all the time 

(c) Others: 

—no diving in the regatta since judges’ opinion, hard to see, takes a 
long time, not maximum participation and very little time to train. 
—Up to individual camp whether held weekly, bi-weekly or monthly. 
—Visitors’ day is a good day to hold the regatta 
—spectators 
—public relations 
—main camp activity on display 
—clean-up previously assigned. 

(d) Rainy weather: 

—should be previously planned, arranged and organized. 

*—suggestions: 

—mock Olympic day 
—films 

—water safety poster contest 
—land demonstration 
—instructional classes 

—skit day (rehearse for one hour, then show) 

—bingo 


DEMONSTRATIONS 

1. Must be highly organized 

2. It must be well rehearsed 


142 


Canadian Camping 



3. Spectator space must be looked after 

4. A good script must be written for the announcer 
3. The demonstration should be short and snappy 

6. There should be no water skiing demonstration unless it can be done 
close to shore. 

7. There should be no spectators allowed on the dock 

8. A vigorous activity should be provided after the show 

9. Rest period is one suggested time for a show 

10. If at all possible use other staff other than waterfront staff 
(Master canoeist, CIT’s, experienced campers 

11. Naturally the ,show must be well supervised by the waterfront director. 

12. Use campers as demonstrators where possible. 

Types 

•—Water safety 

—downproofing (any new items such as Sylvester) 

—canoe pageants vs. demonstrations 
—special safety show such as how to right a sailboat 
—how to set up a campsite 
—how to pack for a trip 
—artificial respiration (history) 

—first-aid 

—care of canoe (1st or 2nd day) 

—use of specialized equipment (paddleboard, skin and scuba) 

—lifejacket demonstration 
—canoe repairing 

—pre-camp demonstrations for the staff i.e. how to teach various 
strokes 

—care of equipment for staff 

To stimulate interest 

—use a skit at lunch hour 
—poster (done by campers, if possible) 

—talk it up in instructional classes 
A demonstration may be used as part of a rainy day programme. 

RECREATION 

(a) Games as part of a lesson: 

—This is very important since it provides the fun in your lesson. 

If your lesson is enjoyable, campers will come back for more and 
they will be more enthusiastic and they will want to learn 
—The game must be related to a skill 

—See the Red Cross Instructor’s Guide and Reference for a list of 
games. 

—Be sure to declare a winner. 

—Over a week period try to make sure that every camper wins at 
least one game 

(b) Games for sectional use: 

—On a hot day a game may be played in the water in place of an 
activity but it must be staffed by sectional staff with the waterfront 
staff acting only in a supervising role. 

—All safety measures must be taken. 

—the following are some suitable games: 


Toronto , Canada, June 1965 


143 



—water polo 
—water basketball 
—water baseball 
—capture the flag 
—log rolling 
—water football 
—canoe tag 

—Be sure that these games are stopped early. Leave them wanting more. 
—Don’t abuse a game (i.e. play it too often) 

(c) Evening dip: 

—potentially dangerous 
-—possible at dusk (not pitch black) 

—do only with a small group .(a cabin group) 

—it is only a dip, not a swim 
—keep it very short (no more than 5 minutes) 

—use the buddy system 

—have at least one staff member in the water at the extreme edge of 
approved area. 

—very enjoyable if it is used sparingly. 

CANOES AND OTHER CRAFT 

(a) Canoeing Games 

—Hunt the whale (G) 

—Tilting (with proper equipment) 

—Flags 

—Follow the leader (lesson — G) 

—Bonker Ball (G)

—Gunwale races 
—Gunwale bobbing 
—Craft paddling 
—Crab splash (N.S.)

—Portage and Paddle race 
—Shake out contests 
—Pony express races 

(b) Special Watercraft activities: 

—Floating campfires 
—Kayak and war canoe trips 
—Canoe sailing 

—Slalom course for canoes and kayaks 
—Building a barge 

—Excursion trips (ray mapping, orienteering) 

(c) Night Campfires: 

—a staff member in each canoe 
—motorboat with light in immediate area 
—flashlight in each canoe 
—good strong platform 


144 


Canadian Camping 



—stem and bow ropes to keep tight circle 
—two roving canoes using staff only 
—lights (floodlights) for disembarking area 

—non-swimmers in war-canoes or rowboats with most qualified staff 
—sectional activity only 

—if there are not enough boats put the campfire out in the lake and 
leave your campers on shore. 


OTHERS 

(a) Special Trips: 

—Skin diving trip 

—small group of boys 

—half day activity 

—two staff in water 

—at least one staff in boat 

—river trip more exciting than lake 

—instructor should go over route first. 

—sailing trip 

—aquaplaning (use 10-18 HP motor only) 

(b) Miscellaneous: 

—do not hold any underwater races (hyperventilation) 

—do not use canoes for obstacle races 
—do not encourage outside competitions 

—interference with regular activity 
—inconvenience and cost of travelling 

—often good-will between camps is destroyed 
—What is gained?

SKILL

WITH PACK and PADDLE 

by ]. D. Scott, Camp Wanapitci. 


So your camp director has decided 
that your camp is going to take part 
in the Centenary Journey Explora¬ 
tions? He has also decided that you 
are going to lead this expedition lasting 
some twelve to fourteen days. You’ve 
suddenly realized that you have never 
led a trip longer than six days; you 
feel somewhat overwhelmed, particu¬ 
larly by the many, many details to 
which you must attend. Herewith a 
few suggestions: 

To begin with, a probable itinerary 
is a Must. This requires good maps 
of a reasonably large scale for the 
entire route. In planning a trip from 
maps, many things must be considered. 
Through what type of country will you 
travel? Can staple foods, such as 
bread, be obtained along the route? 
Are camp sites easily available? If 
river travel is involved, can you and 
your campers handle rapids ‘going 
down’; or are you ‘going up’ and so 
will have to pull or portage all the 
way? (Perhaps your director forbids 
running white water,—best check with 
him to be sure.) Are there many long 
portages? And on and on and on into 
the long, long night! 

Once the itinerary is set, attention 
can be turned to other matters. Select¬ 
ing campers (and staff) for a lengthy 
trip, is not to be taken lightly. Keep 
this in mind: in order that a trip be a 
happy, memorable experience, every¬ 
body must work well together. The 
campers and staff will be in close con¬ 
tact for a considerable length of time. 
There is no place for petty jealousies, 
or the slacker who does not pull his 
load at all times, be it paddling, por¬ 
taging or working at the campsite. 


A long trip can be an un-nerving 
experience for staff members. To be 
continually responsible for the camp¬ 
ers, twenty-four hours a day, builds up 
tension and is a strain on the nervous 
system. It seems advisable that there 
be at least two staff on any trip for 
this reason alone, not to mention 
many others including safety. A second 
staff member provides release from 
tensions since you can talk to him, 
share responsibilities, consult each 
other, etc. Again, the two staff mem¬ 
bers must work well together and be 
companionable. 

The food for a long trip soon 
readies mountainous proportions. It 
must all be packed away in packsacks 
for portaging, along with bedding and 
other necessary equipment. Packing 
should be done in a systematic way so 
that individual items can be located 
without unpacking everything. The 
best method seems to be to divide the 
food and equipment into as many 
roughly-equal portions as there are 
packs and work from there. (You need 
as many packs as there are persons on 
the trip, less the number of canoes you 
are taking.) 

The choice of canoes and equip¬ 
ment is all important because these 
items must stand up to prolonged, 
rugged use. A leaky canoe will bring 
nothing but headaches and discomfort; 
and the packsack whose straps break 
on the first or second portage, is 
absolutely useless! 

Jf, on your proposed trip, you ex¬ 
pect that you may run into portions of 
rivers or lakes choked with logs being 
floated to a mill, check. Lands and 
Forests Officers can usually supply this 


146 


Canadian Camping 



information along with the name of 
the company. Lumber companies by 
federal law, must provide transporta¬ 
tion round such obstacles when it is 
necessary to block a navigable water¬ 
way. Most companies co-operate in 
this regard — provided the Woods 
Supervisor or Logging Superintendent 
knows of your intended arrival well in 
advance. These Logging Company 
employees are excellent sources of local 
information. 

If a return trip by train is involved, 
find out what time the train departs 
and on which days of the week, during 
the initial planning. Also arrange to 
pay for all tickets and excess baggage 
charges (the canoes) BEFORE leaving 
camp, to avoid carrying large sums of 
camp money. The railway will even 
make arrangements so that it is un¬ 
necessary for you to carry your tickets. 
If you are to be met by the camp 
truck, be very sure that both you and 
the driver know the exact time, day 
and spot at which the pick-up is to 
occur. Give the driver WRITTEN 
instructions. 

While you are on route make a 
practice of letting your director know 
of your progress. This puts his mind 
at rest and also keeps those at camp 
interested. A large map of your entire 
route posted in the dining room or 
lodge, arouses interest, and the camp 
can follow your progress if pins 
are used to mark the route and moved 
along as your news comes in! 

Having arranged the route, chosen 
the equipment, packed the food and 
attended to the numerous other neces¬ 
sary details, you’re off. Enjoy your¬ 
self, and don’t forget that your Pro¬ 
vincial Centennial Committee wants a 
detailed log of your encounters en 
route! 


John Scott is the new Chairman of 
Ontario section of the Cross-Canada 
Centenary Canoe Journey. He is eager 


to keep in touch with all provincial 
projects in this area. 

An observation made recently by 
Bruce West in his regular column in 
The Globe and Mail , Toronto, makes 
us feel we are on the right track when 
we plan in future issues of CANADIAN 
CAMPING to have what we shall 
probably call “Wilderness Corner”. 

One of the main ideas of camping is 
to get back to the simple—and some¬ 
times inconvenient—life. There’s some¬ 
thing in some of us which rebels at the 
growing trend toward making every¬ 
thing pushbutton handy. We live in 
an age when so much is done by the 
punch of a button or the click of a 
switch. It makes for a great deal of 
comfort, but the inner man often 
finds himself hungering for the feeling 
that he’s doing something on his own 
for a change. 

“The smoke from a campfire may 
smart his eyes and the cutting of the 
wood for it may make him sweat, but 
when it is finally all glowing and 
blazing and merrily snapping there’s 
something deeply satisfying about it 
that can never be matched by a ther¬ 
mostatically controlled oil burner. 

“Carrying a pail of water from the 
well helps restore your sense of values 
because it gives you a better idea of 
how important fresh water can be. 
When we casually turn a tap for a 
glass of fresh water we often forget 
that this is a luxury enjoyed by com¬ 
paratively few people in the world. 

“Naturally, not many of us would 
care to live in such a basic manner 
throughout the year and I’m not 
knocking the blessings which have been 
given us by modern science and tech¬ 
nology. I’m merely suggesting that 
there is a certain therapeutic value in 
going without them for a few days and 
those of us who would cart them 
along or have them provided for us 
at a campsite are missing the whole 
point of a visit to the great outdoors.” 


Toronto , Canada , June 1965 


147 



CRAFTS, ANYONE? 

by Maty Paton, Camp Onazvaw 


LINO - CUTS 

Use battleship linoleum and speed- 
ball cutters or cut with rib of an 
umbrella. 

1. Draw a design on a piece of lino¬ 
leum. 

2. Gouge out areas you do not want 
printed. 

3. Roll printing ink on the linoleum 
with a roller (Brayer) or brush. 

4. Place paper on the inked linoleum. 

5. Rub with a wooden spoon. 

Lift paper gently and you have a 
linoleum print. Try different kinds of 
paper and printing ink (water or oil 
base will do). 

LEAF PRINTING 

1. Collect as many types of plants and 
leaves as you find interesting. 

2. Paint over with tempera paint, or 
roll printing ink on leaves with 
roller. 

3. Press with painted leaf (paint side 
down) to a sheet of blank paper. 

4. Cover with newspaper and press 
with the palm of your hand. 

5. Repeat, using different colours, 
leaves, plants, till desired pattern 
is obtained. 

CARDBOARD PRINTING 

1. Gut out cardboard shapes. 

2. Paste them on a piece of heavy 
cardboard. 

3. Paint the cardboard, or roll print¬ 
ing ink on with roller (Brayer). 

4. Place newsprint on top and rub 
with a spoon. 

5. Lift gently and now you have a 
cardboard print. 

COLLAGES 

1. Paste pieces of cloth, paper, maca¬ 
roni, seeds, beans, or anything you 
like on a plain background. 


2. You can form a picture or design 
with paint or ink. 

3. Just use your own imagination, and 
you can create your very own 
collage 1 

PAPER MOSAICS 

t. Cut different colours of construc¬ 
tion paper into small squares, and 
keep them in separate cups. Make 
your design with the squares on a 
piece of heavy cardboard. 

2. After you have made your design 
with the squares, paste each square 
down, making sure there is space 
around each one. Very colourful! 

BATIK 

Materials required: 

Paraffin Wax 

Cloth (washed to remove sizing) 
white or unbleached cotton. Old 
sheet or pillowcase is satisfactory. 
Paint brushes (artists brushes) 

Dye—cloth dye. We used RIT. 
Iron 

Newsprint or newspaper or solvent 
(i.e. carbon tetrachloride) 
Double-boiler for melting wax or 
equivalent (105 oz. can for water, 
or 48 oz. can for wax) 

Pail or tub for dyes. 

Stove or hot plate 
Wooden frame (depends on size of 
cloth—we have used 2" x 4" wood 
for frame) 

Procedure: 

1. Melt wax in double-boiler. 

2. Tack cloth over wooden frame. 

3. Paint design with very hot wax on 
the cloth. 

4. Dip cloth in prepared dye (cooled) 
and stir around with a stick. 

5. Take out and hang up to dry. 

6. After it is dry, remove wax with 
solvent or press between news¬ 
paper with warm iron. 


148 


Canadian Camping 



7. Other colours can be added by re¬ 
waxing. The parts you don’t wish 
coloured should be waxed. Remem¬ 
ber, if you have yellow and add 
red, the dyed yellow will become 
orange if it is not waxed carefully 
before dipping into the red! 

CRAYON DRIP 

Materials required: L 

Candle, paper (e.g. newsprint), 
crayons (suggest Peacock Box of 
48 crayons gives widest variety of 
colours). 

1. Take paper off crayons — can be 
broken up. 

2. Light candle. Hold the end of the 
crayon in the flame. 

3. Drip hot crayon on paper—it’s fun! 

NATURE PLAQUES 

Materials required: 

Pieces of wood (e.g. *4" plywood, 
size 12" x 6" or maybe 3"x6"); 
dried natural materials; glue; 
clear spray, or coloured sprays 

I such as silver, red, etc. - 

Procedure: 

1. Sand plywood. 

2. Arrange natural materials and glue 
them in place. 

3. Spray with clear or coloured spray. 

BEAN AND SEE£> JEWELRY j 

1. Soak beans and seeds overnight in 
dye (we use RIT). 

2. Rinse before using. 

3. String beans and seeds while soft. 
Remember you cannot keep them 
damp too long as they will 
germinate. 

4. Dry remaining seeds and beans and 
use for collages (see above). 

GLASS MOSAICS 

Materials required: L 

Pieces of wood of different sizes (e.g. 

J4" plywood size 12" x 8"). 

Scraps of coloured glass; brass nails 


(small head); shellac or clear 
plastic spray. 

Procedure: 

1. Sand and shellac or spray wood. 

2. Make design on wood using differ¬ 
ent pieces of coloured glass. 

3. Tack pieces of glass gently in place 
with brass nails. 

SOURCES OF SUPPLY: You will 
find that macaroni can be bought in 
lots of different shapes and sizes in 
Italian grocery stores. Feed and Seed 
stores supply all sorts of seeds and 
beans. You will find squash seeds, 
pumpkin seeds, lima beans, peas, 
Indian corn all useful in these crafts. 

BOOKS (May be found in some 
libraries) : 

DICTIONARY OF DISCARDS by 
Frank Rich; Association Press, $2.00. 

EXPERIENCES IN CREATIVE 
ART TEACHING by Victor D’Amico; 
Doubleday, $3.25. 

CREATIVE CRAFTS FOR CAMP¬ 
ERS by Catharine Hammett and Carol 
Horrocks; Association Press, $8.75. 

THE BOOK OF ARTS AND 
CRAFTS by Marguerite Ickes and Esh 
Reba; Association Press. 

Pocket Books:

CRAFT has been re-issued, 35^.

come in a 65^ edition on NATIVE 
CRAFTS, CRAFTS AND HOBBIES.

Dansville, N.Y. issues a magazine and 
also in their Instructor Handbook

Toronto , Canada , June 1965

from pae 129 

make bed-rolls; why do we need a 
ground sheet? Explain the necessity of 
preparations for a comfortable night’s 
sleep. We will need to store our food. 
How can we build a “refrigerator” in 
the campsite: how do we keep our

campers understand the importance of

And now our campsite is neat and 
safe, our tent is secure and our bed¬ 
rolls and sleeping bags are arranged 
for the night. We have cooked, eaten, 
and cleaned up after our supper. The 
glorious sunset has faded into a black 
velvety sky with the stars twinkling 
above us. We are gathered around 
our campfire until bed-time. The 
counsellor or camp director will tell us 
Indian stories or star legends; we will 
sing our favourite camp songs and 
quietly talk to our friends as the 
embers glow and slowly fade away. 

All this is Day Camp!
